newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania leaders to seek aid as rivals snap back.
newsitem.headline: Albania leaders to seek aid as rivals snap back.

text.p: Albania's new prime minister, Fatos Nano, went to Italy on Wednesday for a conference of international donors that will discuss how to rebuild Europe's poorest economy, which has been shattered by months of unrest.

"We shall define the priorities of our work, the framework of talks with world institutions and ways of communicating with donors, banks and other governments...so that our programme can be applied immediately," Nano told reporters before leaving Tirana airport.

Albania is seeking international assistance to reconstruct the Balkan nation, which was in a dire state even before violence, looting and general anarchy broke out in March in response to the collapse of a number of shaky pyramid investment schemes.
Nano is due to meet Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and will hold roundtable talks with ministers.

"This is a preparatory conference for a high-level donors' conference in October. It will decide the priorities for the areas and types of international assistance," his spokesman, Vladimir Prela, said.

Albania's parliament on Wednesday began debating a draft law to regulate the country's remaining high-yield investment schemes to prevent a recurrence of the pyramid scheme scandal that toppled the Democratic Party government.

Voters threw their support behind Nano and the Socialists, reformed successors of the hardline communists who were ousted after 45 years in power in 1990, in an early general election last month. The Democratic Party lost nearly 100 of its parliamentary seats in the vote.
President Sali Berisha resigned a week ago, saying he was unable to work with a leftist administration.
On Tuesday, parliament, dominated by the Socialist Party and its allies with 119 seats in the 155-seat chamber, gave resounding backing to Nano's policies to restore order.

Democratic Party secretary-general Genc Pollo told a news conference on Wednesday that Nano's programme would deepen the economic crisis and further impoverish the Albanian people, triggering disillusion and social upheaval.

"A programme which foresees an increase of taxes, the devaluation of the lek currency and inflation will deteriorate the situation, further impoverish our people and deter eventual foreign investors," Pollo said.
He added that the Democrats would continue to boycott what he called "the parliament of Kalashnikovs", where the Democrats hold just 27 seats.

The international community, which helped Albania hold early elections aimed at ending the months of unrest, has said continuing a policy of national unity is a must if foreign aid is to be delivered.
Pollo said the Socialists sought revenge and would divide the country.

"We are deeply concerned that members of the new government plan to launch attacks against Democratic Party supporters in the north under the pretext of fighting criminal gangs," Pollo said, referring to comments by Interior Minister Neritan Ceka.

Ceka told parliament that police had clear evidence that former intelligence service (Shik) officers and officials of the former administration were intent on provoking trouble in northern Albania to oust the newly-elected government.
"Such a statement shows the revenge and hallucinations of the former communists and may destabilise the situation in the country," Pollo said.
